title: Whom to Query for What: Adaptive Group Elicitation via Multi-Turn LLM Interactions
one_liner: Use limited question rounds on the most informative people and questions so group-level properties can be inferred with less survey budget.
lead: This paper studies how to ask a group only a small number of questions while still recovering a population-level property such as political leaning or opinion distribution. The challenge is twofold: each round must choose both what to ask and whom to ask, and some responses may be missing. The paper proposes a multi-turn selection rule that chooses question-person subsets to reduce uncertainty as quickly as possible under a fixed budget.

problem.h2: Why fixed surveys waste limited question budget
paras: A standard survey often asks the same questions to the same style of respondent whether or not those answers are still informative. That wastes budget because later rounds should depend on what is already known.

The problem becomes harder when some responses are missing. Then the system must choose questions and respondents while also filling gaps in partial group information. The paper treats this as an adaptive information-gathering problem where each round should reduce uncertainty about a group-level target as much as possible.

callout.b: The paper's move in one sentence.
callout.html: At each round, choose the question and respondent subset with the highest expected information gain, while using a group model to combine and complete the partial answers already observed.

panels.title: 1. The group is large
panels.viz_args: Many people, many possible questions, limited time and money.
panels.caption: The budget is tight because not everyone can answer every question.

panels.title: 2. A fixed questionnaire starts asking blindly
panels.viz_args: The same prompts go to broad respondent sets even after some answers become predictable.
panels.caption: That wastes rounds because some question-person pairs add little new information.

panels.title: 3. Partial answers reveal where uncertainty remains
panels.viz_args: Some regions of the group are still unclear and some respondents did not answer.
panels.caption: The next round should target those uncertain regions because they matter most for the final estimate.

panels.title: 4. The method picks the next best pair
panels.viz_args: Choose a question and a subset of respondents that are expected to reduce uncertainty the most.
panels.caption: This saves budget because the system asks only where the answer is most informative.

panels.title: 5. The group property becomes clear
panels.caption: After several adaptive rounds, the target group quantity is estimated from fewer total responses.

steps.text: Collect the responses already observed so the next choice can depend on what is known and what is missing.
Use a group relation model to combine observed answers and fill gaps because missing responses should still influence later selections.
Estimate expected information gain for each possible next query so the budget goes to the most informative option.
Send the selected question only to the selected respondents because broad asking is often unnecessary.
Fold the new answers back into the group model so the next round starts from a smaller uncertainty region.

paras: The paper changes the survey policy. Instead of a fixed questionnaire over a fixed respondent set, it uses a sequential policy that chooses both the next question and the next respondent subset.
object.object: the query policy for group-level information gathering

hidden.name: how much one additional question to one subset will reduce uncertainty about the group target
paras: The central hidden quantity is information value under a budget. A question may be useful for one respondent group and nearly useless for another, depending on what has already been learned and which responses are still missing.

The paper estimates this quantity with an information-gain objective plus a group model for partial data. That pairing is important because uncertainty should be measured at the group level, not only at the individual answer level.

heat.caption: The high cells mark places where one more question is likely to shrink uncertainty about the population target.

reads.html: The hidden quantity is how much this exact question to this exact subset will help us understand the whole group because some answers sharply reduce group uncertainty while others mostly repeat what is already known.
The method chooses queries by expected information gain over the hidden group property while using partial group structure to handle missing answers.

mechanism.h2: Why adaptive question and respondent selection helps
paras: Adaptive selection helps because later rounds should exploit earlier answers. Once one region of the group is predictable, spending more questions there adds little value, so the policy should shift budget toward the people and prompts that still change the group estimate.

The group model matters because missing responses are structured rather than random noise. By combining related respondents, the method can estimate what is already partly known and then ask only where the missing uncertainty is still large.

stages.s: Observed answers, missing entries, and target group quantity
Score question-person subsets by expected information gain
Ask the best subset and update the model
Smaller group-estimate error because each round targets the most informative unanswered region

math.h2: Choose the next round by uncertainty reduction
math.words: At each round, prefer the question and respondent subset that most reduces uncertainty about the target group property per unit of budget spent.
math.equation: pick_next = argmax over (question, subset) of information_gain(question, subset) / cost(question, subset)
symbols: the next question and respondent subset selected for one round
expected reduction in uncertainty about the target group quantity
budget consumed by asking that question to that subset

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Question A to subset 1 reduces expected uncertainty by 12 units and costs 6 response slots.
Question B to subset 2 reduces expected uncertainty by 10 units and costs 3 response slots.
A gives gain per cost 2.0, while B gives gain per cost about 3.3.
The policy chooses B because B shrinks uncertainty more for each unit of budget.

math.note: The real method uses a richer estimator, but this ratio captures the main idea that adaptive elicitation should spend budget where uncertainty falls fastest.

charts.title: Fixed questionnaire baseline
charts.note: The baseline wastes questions because it does not adapt to what the earlier rounds already revealed.

charts.title: Adaptive group elicitation
charts.note: The paper reports better prediction under tight budgets because the method asks more informative question-person pairs and uses partial group structure to guide the choice.

items.b: The uncertainty estimate can be wrong.
items.html: If the group model misreads which region is uncertain, the policy may spend budget on the wrong people because the expected gain calculation started from a bad belief state.
If nonresponse follows a hidden social pattern, simple completion rules can mislead the estimator because the missing answers are not just random blanks.
An early question may influence how a person answers later prompts, so the sequential policy may alter the data-generating process because interaction itself has effects.
The paper is useful because it treats elicitation as a budgeted decision problem instead of a fixed form.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small opinion dataset with a known group target and artificial budget limits. Compare a fixed survey policy against an adaptive one that chooses both the next question and the next respondent subset after each round, while some answers are hidden to mimic missing responses.

The demo should show lower target-estimation error under the same budget because the adaptive policy focuses queries where uncertainty is still large and stops spending questions on predictable parts of the group.
demo.closing: A convincing demo proves that better group estimates can come from asking fewer but better targeted questions because the budget is spent where one more answer reduces uncertainty the most.
